title: Engineered two-photon dissipative confinement of a Kerr-cat qubit using SISIS quantum circuit refrigerator
authors: Shumpei Masuda, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, Shuji Nakamura, Daichi Sugiyama, Akiyoshi Tomonaga
abstract: Kerr-cat qubits realized in periodically driven superconducting nonlinear resonators are a promising platform for quantum information processing with biased noise. Pure dephasing in such systems induces leakage out of the qubit subspace, motivating the use of quantum circuit refrigeration (QCR) to remove excess excitations. While conventional superconductor--insulator--normal-metal--insulator--superconductor (SINIS)-based QCRs can suppress leakage via single-photon absorption, they also enhance QCR-induced phase-flip errors. Here we investigate a QCR based on a superconductor--insulator--superconductor--insulator--superconductor (SISIS) junction coupled to a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). We show that a SISIS-based QCR can operate in a regime where single-photon processes are suppressed while two-photon absorption dominates. As a result, the proposed SISIS-based QCR achieves strong suppression of dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the increase in phase-flip errors associated with QCR operation. These results demonstrate that the proposed SISIS-based QCR provides an effective approach for mitigating leakage while limiting QCR-induced phase-flip errors in Kerr-cat qubits.
summary: This paper proposes using a Superconductor-Insulator-Superconductor-Insulator-Superconductor (SISIS) junction as a Quantum Circuit Refrigerator (QCR) for Kerr-cat qubits. By tuning the bias voltage, the system can be engineered to favor two-photon absorption, which efficiently removes leakage errors while crucially suppressing the phase-flip errors common in other QCR designs. This offers a robust pathway for improving qubit coherence in superconducting quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of mitigating leakage errors in Kerr-cat qubits caused by pure dephasing while simultaneously minimizing the increase in phase-flip errors induced by Quantum Circuit Refrigeration (QCR).
main_result: A novel SISIS-based QCR operating in a two-photon absorption regime effectively suppresses dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the detrimental phase-flip errors compared to conventional SINIS-based methods.
method: The authors derive the system dynamics using a master equation approach, calculating transition rates via Fermi's golden rule applied to quasiparticle tunneling processes.
model_or_system: The system models a Kerr-cat qubit (KPO) coupled to a superconducting island via a SISIS junction. The dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian and analyzed through the evolution of the reduced density matrix.
key_observables: Population of excited (leakage) states, population of $|\varphi_0angle$, population of $|\varphi_\alphaangle$, and the relative rates of phase-flip versus deexcitation transitions.
important_parameters: The applied bias voltage ($V_B$), the tunnel resistance ($R_T$), and the ratio of two-photon to single-photon absorption rates.
main_assumptions: The analysis employs the Born–Markov approximation and treats quasiparticle tunneling perturbatively, assuming the superconducting density of states dictates the tunneling rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level diagrams showing the suppression of single-photon processes in favor of two-photon processes. Time evolution plots compare state populations under varying tunnel resistances ($R_T$) for both SISIS and SINIS configurations.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem and the SISIS mechanism. It then develops the theoretical framework by deriving the master equation and calculating transition rates based on the junction structure. Finally, it analyzes the time evolution by simulating state populations under varying critical parameters like $R_T$.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical blueprint for engineering error mitigation in superconducting qubits by exploiting specific quantum tunneling mechanisms (two-photon vs. single-photon) within a superconducting circuit refrigerator.
